name: Proto-porcelain in Shang China
summary: Potters in China began making proto-porcelain, a glazed ceramic fired above 1200 degrees Celsius, during the Shang dynasty, about 1700 to 1027 BCE.
description: Proto-porcelain, a high-fired ceramic with a lime-rich glaze that matures above 1200 degrees Celsius, began to appear in China during the Shang dynasty and became more widespread under the Zhou. Most finds come from mound tombs and kiln sites in the lower Yangtze region; sherds from production sites at Deqing in Zhejiang have bodies of local porcelain stone and glazes made by deliberately applying wood ash.

impact.note: Scored on the general view, not on the cited page: high-fired glazed wares became the ceramics of China and its neighbours for generations (reach 2), were at this stage a better pot rather than a new capability (depth 1), and the whole line of celadon and porcelain grew from them (generativity 2).

date.label: Shang dynasty, c. 1700–1027 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Proto-porcelain, a high-fired lime-rich glazed ceramic, began to appear in China during the Shang dynasty, c. 1700 to 1027 BCE.

evidence.supports: began to appear in China during the Shang dynasty (c. 1700 to 1027 BC)

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Read the Shang kiln site reports (Piaoshan, Beijiashan, Nanshan in northern Zhejiang) to date the earliest proto-porcelain kilns more closely than the dynasty's span.
Lay out the dragon kiln's origin and the later steps to Eastern Han celadon and to white porcelain, linking to the Xing and Gongyi whiteware records rather than duplicating them.
Decide whether earlier high-fired wares elsewhere (for example Harappan stoneware bangles) bear on whether this is the first known record of the concept.

research.note: The thesis abstract says the differences in firing temperature and composition underpin the suggestion that the Chinese lime-rich glazes are an independent invention, but that is a hedged remark about the glazes read in an abstract only, and it does not say these were the earliest high-fired glazed ceramics anywhere.
